heading: # Preface {.unnumbered}
text: This is the central question of the book: **what shapes a choice before it is made, and how can we use that understanding to choose better?**

heading: ## Examine the comparison, measure, and estimate {#read-each-boundary-in-four-moves}
text: For example, a person who rejects an unequal offer might dislike inequality, want to punish the proposer, or be concerned about reputation. The rejection alone does not identify the motive. A convincing explanation needs a comparison that helps distinguish the alternatives, rather than a new label for the same observation.

heading: ### Two examples from commercial practice {#two-suggestive-cases-with-weaker-evidence}
text: The next two cases suggest useful mechanisms, but their evidence is weaker than the controlled comparisons above. Read them as questions to investigate, not established estimates of what an arrow or a product name will cause.

heading: ### Two examples from commercial practice {#two-suggestive-cases-with-weaker-evidence}
text: News reports in 1997 linked rising Mars-bar sales to publicity around NASA's Pathfinder mission. Repeated references to *Mars* offer an intuitive hypothesis: the product name may have become easier to retrieve without any change in the chocolate. The available sales account cannot establish that causal connection (Grant, 1997).[^ch01-mars-sales]

heading: ### Two examples from commercial practice {#two-suggestive-cases-with-weaker-evidence}
text: Berger and Fitzsimons (2008) later used the association to motivate experiments on environmental cues and choice. The distinction is worth keeping: a memorable story suggests a mechanism; a suitable comparison tests it. [*Priming, Fluency, and Familiarity*](13-accessibility-familiarity-and-ease.qmd#accessibility-familiarity-and-ease) develops the experimentally grounded account.

heading: # Building a Better Decision
text: A comparison table should help her choose the job that best fits her life. But without the missing information, it cannot establish whether the working conditions are sustainable. Its fixed columns may also hide a better possibility: changing an offer before accepting it. Her income, learning, and daily life depend on more than which column wins. What can she negotiate, what would each commitment give up, and what does she need to learn before deciding?

heading: ## Construct the feasible set
text: Ask: **What would have to change for this option to become feasible, and who could change it?** The answer might identify a negotiation, permission, investment, or redesign. It might also confirm that the boundary is fixed.

heading: ## Use proportionate analysis
text: Bounded rationality recognizes that search, attention, time, memory, and computation are scarce (Simon, 1955, 1956). People often **satisfice**: they search until an alternative meets an aspiration level rather than proving global optimality. That can be procedurally rational when further search costs more than it is likely to improve the decision.

heading: ## How sensory and measurement limits shape the evidence {#available-information-is-not-complete-information}
text: The practical lesson extends to what our records let us know. A confident presentation is immediately visible; long-run reliability requires observations across time. Attendance can be counted without establishing attention, and prevention costs can be recorded without revealing the harm prevented. Instruments, records, and models extend what we can observe, but their coverage remains partial and their results still need interpretation. Ask: **What consequential information is absent from the current sensory, metric, or reporting system?**

heading: ## Anticipating the body's needs {#anticipating-bodily-needs}
text: When the body loses water, changes in fluid concentration and circulating volume help generate thirst. Yet a drink can relieve that feeling quickly, while absorption and the restoration of fluid balance are still under way. Feeling less thirsty does not mean that a water deficit has already been corrected throughout the body. In a small human experiment, thirst fell within minutes of drinking; even a much smaller amount reduced reported thirst, although its hormonal effects differed (Williams et al., 1989).

heading: ## Anticipating the body's needs {#anticipating-bodily-needs}
text: The visual and bodily examples share a useful lesson: what we experience depends on incoming signals together with the context in which the nervous system interprets them. Their mechanisms need not be identical. The thirst experiments provide evidence of anticipatory regulation; the toilet example points to learned cues and attention. [Chapter 5](05-expectations-when-predictions-become-causes.qmd#illness-after-a-deadline) considers a more uncertain case: feeling ill only after a demanding period ends, and why its timing alone cannot establish an expectation effect.

heading: ### Changing the current interpretation and changing the model {.unlisted}
text: A **prompt** can supply instructions, examples, facts, and a conversation history. It plays a role analogous to contextual cues: it helps establish what the current task is and which responses fit. The model's learned parameters supply enduring structure; its temporary internal representations depend on the input being processed. During ordinary prompting, those representations change without retraining the parameters. This distinction underlies **in-context learning**: examples can alter how a task is performed without a training update to the model's weights (Brown et al., 2020).

heading: ### Changing the current interpretation and changing the model {.unlisted}
text: The word *weight* can obscure this distinction. A model's **parameters** encode learned relationships; the **weight given to evidence** concerns how strongly an observation should influence the current judgment. A knowledgeable person can give decisive weight to a clear observation that contradicts an expectation. Having learned more does not mechanically mean assigning less weight to new evidence.

heading: ### Change the question—and then seek evidence {.unlisted}
text: Changing the frame can open another possibility. It cannot settle which possibility is correct. That requires evidence beyond the plausibility of the account. [Chapter 42](42-data-driven-decision-making.qmd#ai-workbench) builds on this distinction: generative AI can help articulate options and questions, while predictions used for consequential choices need validation and the values guiding those choices need explicit human judgment.

heading: ## When a forecast enters the causal system
text: An expectation can change either the evidence we notice or the outcome itself. If the manager overlooks a junior colleague's good ideas, the problem is **confirmation bias**, examined in [Chapter 10](10-beliefs-that-defend-themselves.qmd#expectations-and-confirmation). If close supervision removes the colleague's opportunity to take initiative, the expectation has entered the causal system. Both processes can operate together. This chapter asks the second question: **What changed because someone held the expectation?**

heading: ## When a forecast enters the causal system
text: Expectations can also prevent their predicted outcomes. A warning about failure may prompt preparation that makes the project succeed. Such a **self-defeating prediction** can be useful even though the forecasted event never occurs. The key question is whether people reacted in a way that changed the system.

heading: ## When a forecast enters the causal system
text: Non-occurrence does not show that the warning was irrational.

heading: ## Expectation in the body
text: **Placebo effects** are changes attributable to treatment context, including expectations and learning, beyond the specific action of the treatment. **Nocebo effects** are adverse changes attributable to such contextual processes. They can accompany active treatment as well as an inert intervention (Benedetti, 2008; Colloca & Barsky, 2020; Colloca & Miller, 2011). Improvement in a placebo group alone does not establish a placebo effect: natural recovery, regression to the mean, and other influences may also contribute.

heading: ## Ability beliefs and performance
text: Meta-analytic work finds modest, context-dependent mindset effects (Sisk et al., 2018). Yeager and colleagues (2019) found that a brief intervention raised end-of-ninth-grade GPAs in core subjects among lower-achieving US students by an estimated 0.10 points on a four-point scale relative to the control group. In the follow-up covering both lower- and higher-achieving students, advanced mathematics enrollment in tenth grade was 36% in the intervention group, compared with 33% in the control group. The grade benefit depended partly on school context. The practical lesson is to pair beliefs about development with real opportunities, strategies, support, and feedback.

heading: ## Learning goals
text: Neuroeconomic evidence links valuation to interacting systems rather than one literal “value center” (Bartra et al., 2013; Clithero & Rangel, 2014; Levy & Glimcher, 2012; Rangel et al., 2008). The research note near the end explains why a neural response alone cannot establish what someone truly values.

heading: ## Research note: are needs a hierarchy? {#research-note-are-needs-a-hierarchy-title}
text: The central question is: **Which motive gives this option its appeal now, and will that motive matter over the period affected by the choice?**

heading: ## Research note: arousal and impatience can come apart
text: Kim and Zauberman (2013) proposed a different route. In their studies, sexual cues made future intervals feel subjectively longer, and this change was associated with greater preference for smaller-sooner hypothetical monetary rewards. On this account, the delayed reward did not necessarily become less desirable in itself. It lost decision weight because the wait separating the chooser from it expanded psychologically. The distinction matters: an intervention aimed at reward appetite would miss a change in perceived temporal distance.

heading: ## Research note: arousal and impatience can come apart
text: The evidence requirements in @tbl-contextual-cues-and-waiting show why arousal or neural reward responses alone cannot establish a change in intertemporal choice. A behavioral shift may instead reflect perceived time or a starting-point bias toward immediate rewards. The designs help distinguish these pathways.

heading: ## Using valuation wisely
text: This distinction becomes central when an organization uses AI. An accurate prediction cannot by itself establish which outcome is worth predicting, whose welfare should count, or how costly different mistakes would be. [Chapter 42](42-data-driven-decision-making.qmd#ai-target-variable-problem) turns this chapter's valuation audit into questions about a model's target and the action it supports. Making prediction cheaper increases the practical importance of stating and examining those priorities.

heading: ## Research Lens: how interacting brain systems represent value
text: The **common-currency hypothesis** proposes that some neural signals represent subjective value on a scale that permits comparison across different kinds of reward (Levy & Glimcher, 2012). This is a claim about a possible comparison code, not a claim that all values are money, that every region computes the same quantity, or that a brain scan reveals the morally correct choice.

heading: ## Research Lens: how interacting brain systems represent value
text: does not show that the region contains a unique psychological function.

heading: # The Narrator After Choice
text: This is the experimental logic of **choice blindness** (Johansson et al., 2005). Some people notice the switch. When it goes unnoticed, the reasons offered afterward raise a difficult question: how do we know whether an explanation recovers a cause or constructs a plausible story? The distinction matters whenever we use an account of a decision to repeat a success, repair a failure, or assign responsibility.

heading: ## The benefits and costs of deliberate thought {#slow-thinking-is-powerful-expensive-and-often-late}
text: The effort involved can also influence whether we choose to think further. Kool and colleagues (2010) let participants choose between two on-screen decks of cards. Each card required a simple judgment: whether a number was even or whether it was below five. One deck required frequent switches between these rules; the other usually repeated the previous rule. Participants tended to favor the deck requiring fewer switches. Across the paper's experiments, avoiding errors or finishing sooner could not fully explain the preference for less demanding tasks. Being capable of deliberate thought does not guarantee that we will engage it. The practical aim is to direct that effort toward judgments where checking could make a worthwhile difference.

heading: ### Some systems explicitly search among alternatives {.unlisted}
text: The idea of a model “prompting itself” is especially concrete in systems with a search procedure around the LLM. **Tree of Thoughts**, for example, generates candidate intermediate steps, evaluates alternatives, and searches forward or backtracks among them (Yao et al., 2023). Here, a control procedure organizes repeated model calls. Other reasoning systems develop a single extended sequence; a reasoning label alone does not establish that a separate controller compares multiple branches.

heading: ### Some systems explicitly search among alternatives {.unlisted}
text: The functional resemblance to metacognition lies in treating an intermediate answer as something to examine and potentially revise. It does not establish human-like awareness or make the AI architecture an implementation of the psychological System 1/System 2 distinction.

heading: ## How beliefs shape the test {#expectations-and-confirmation}
text: [Chapter 5](05-expectations-when-predictions-become-causes.qmd#when-a-forecast-enters-the-causal-system) asked whether acting on an expectation changes what happens. This chapter asks whether a belief receives a fair test. In the app example, the colleagues can interpret the same customer comments differently even when neither has changed the product or the customers' experience. That is a problem of inference.

heading: ## Optional research note: can a flattering belief help?
text: When an excessively favorable belief concerns future outcomes, it is often called **unrealistic optimism** or **optimism bias**. Hope alone does not establish an error; the forecast needs a defensible accuracy benchmark. The leader can express confidence in the team's capacity to improve while recording a realistic adoption forecast and agreeing when results would require a redesign. [Chapter 15](15-samples-randomness-regression-and-calibration.qmd#confidence-must-face-a-distribution) distinguishes confidence about performance, relative standing, and uncertainty, and shows how to test each.

heading: ## Together or separately: what becomes easy to evaluate? {#evaluation-modes}
text: The **evaluability hypothesis** explains why an attribute can gain weight when a comparison makes its magnitude interpretable. A clean cover supplies its own standard; the usefulness of a word count often requires one. The practical question is whether the comparison reveals something important or merely something easy to rank.

heading: ## Questions that contain an answer
text: The sales team can check its frame by stating which observation would support each explanation. The next section shows why recording observations before asking a leading question matters as well.

heading: ## Reframing decisions in practice {#framing-in-management-negotiation-and-policy}
text: The same care applies in management. A label such as “rightsizing” should not obscure job losses, and calling a workload a “stretch goal” does not establish that it is sustainable. The safeguards in @tbl-15-1 follow what the frame changed: restate equivalent quantities, reopen missing alternatives, or test an implied cause.

heading: ## Accessibility: memory prepares an answer
text: Smith and Vela's (2001) meta-analysis found reliable environmental-context effects, with smaller effects when other retrieval cues were strong or the original setting was mentally reinstated. Failure to retrieve something in one setting is not proof it was never learned.

heading: ## Accessible concepts interpret ambiguity
text: Accessibility can carry affect as well as meaning, and affective-priming tasks have sometimes shifted immediate evaluation in specified laboratory conditions (Fazio et al., 1986; Murphy & Zajonc, 1993). [Chapter 9](09-what-feels-likely-availability-affect-and-resemblance.qmd#when-value-substitutes-for-evidence-affect-answers-first) distinguishes feelings about an option from feelings carried into it. The practical implication is order sensitivity: when an ambiguous target follows an emotional cue, use independent ratings, counterbalancing, a break, or delayed review before treating the evaluation as evidence about the target.

text: Start with a short workplace message: “The new review system is simple, fair, and proven.” Employees need to know what will change and how their performance will be judged. The sentence is fluent, but each adjective substitutes an assurance for something they need to inspect. Consider this fictional redesign:

heading: ## Natural frequencies make Bayes visible
text: Knowing the updating rule does not guarantee that the relevant denominator stays visible. Translating percentages into people makes it easier to inspect who could have produced a positive result.

heading: ## Regression to the mean
text: Regression does not show that an intervention had no effect. It shows why before–after change among units selected for extreme outcomes does not identify the effect by itself. Use comparison groups, repeated pre-periods, credible counterfactuals, and uncertainty intervals. A real treatment effect and regression can occur together.

heading: ### Superstition and the illusion of control {#superstition}
text: A basketball player tosses chalk into the air before a game; a golfer wears red on Sunday. LeBron James’s chalk toss and Tiger Woods’s red shirt are familiar sporting rituals (NBA, 2009; PGA TOUR, 2024). In a humorous interview, Woods recalled winning in red, then unsuccessfully trying blue to challenge his mother’s belief that red was his “power color.” The sequence makes a memorable story, but different tournaments also bring different opponents, conditions, and performances. It cannot establish what the shirt contributed.

heading: ### Superstition and the illusion of control {#superstition}
text: **Superstition** attributes influence to an action or sign without adequate evidence of a causal connection. A ritual alone does not establish such a belief: an athlete might use a familiar routine to prepare or concentrate. The question is whether the claimed influence has a plausible pathway and survives a fair comparison.

heading: ### Superstition and the illusion of control {#superstition}
text: Langer's (1975) classic studies helped establish the topic, but one familiar inference needs care: preferring a lottery ticket one selected does not show a belief that selecting it improved the odds. Preference, ownership, and anticipated regret can also matter. Across 17 experiments with 10,825 participants, Klusowski, Small, and Simmons (2021) found little support for the claim that choice itself creates inflated success expectations when options are functionally identical.

heading: ### Superstition and the illusion of control {#superstition}
text: The lesson for the manager is to measure causal beliefs and compare outcomes, rather than treating active involvement—or recovery after a bad quarter—as evidence of effectiveness.

heading: ## Overconfidence: three different errors {#confidence-must-face-a-distribution}
text: The forms can move in opposite directions. In Moore and Healy's experiments, difficult tasks could produce overestimation of one's score alongside underplacement relative to others; easy tasks could reverse that combination. An error therefore needs a specified task, scale, comparison group, and repeated assessment. A confident manner, an ambitious goal, or one failed prediction cannot establish a general tendency.

heading: ## Research Lens: information protocols change probability puzzles
text: In Monty Hall, seeing two unopened doors can make staying and switching look equally promising. Yet the host’s rule for revealing a goat determines what the reveal tells us: similar-looking endings can carry different evidence. In the standard Monty Hall protocol, a knowledgeable host always reveals a goat behind an unchosen door and always offers a switch; if either goat door could be opened, assume the host chooses between them uniformly at random. Following the unchosen-door branch in @fig-monty-hall-protocol shows why switching wins with probability $2/3$, compared with $1/3$ for staying (Selvin, 1975). If the host instead opens doors or offers a switch selectively, the evidence changes. Likewise, “at least one child is a boy,” “the older child is a boy,” and a parent volunteering “I have a boy” arise from different sampling rules. The transferable question is not the puzzle answer but: **How was this information generated?**

heading: ## Choices under risk, uncertainty, and ambiguity {#opening-puzzle-the-same-expected-value-a-different-choice}
text: For the insurance team, this distinction changes what to investigate. Even a well-estimated frequency of familiar incidents may omit a new kind of attack; a precise average cannot settle whether the model covers the exposure.

heading: ### Curvature and attitudes toward a mean-preserving risk
text: Curvature is local. A function can be concave over one wealth range and different elsewhere. Observing one safe choice does not establish a stable trait across stakes, domains, or reference points.

heading: # Prospect Theory
text: This chapter asks how a model could explain that reversal. If the comparison begins with everyone dying, 200 survivors appear as a gain worth protecting. If it begins with everyone surviving, 400 deaths appear as a loss that a gamble might avoid. Representing the outcome is already part of evaluating it.

heading: ## One applied audit across three settings
text: Higher enrollment alone does not show that the default serves the worker. The employer must be able to justify the implied recommendation for the people receiving it, while preserving the usable exit and adjustment options.

heading: ### Endowment effects: how ownership changes valuation {#endowment-effects-giving-up-is-not-the-same-as-owning}
text: Loss aversion offers one explanation: giving up an owned mug is coded as a loss. But a willingness-to-accept/willingness-to-pay gap can also reflect transaction costs, income effects, misunderstanding, strategic answers, attachment, or different information and attention among buyers and sellers. The gap is not a direct measure of the loss-aversion parameter.

heading: ### Small samples can erase rare events
text: The slowly falling one-percent curve in @fig-experience-rare-event-sampling shows why an uneventful sample can coexist with a real rare-event risk. The following sections examine how selective exposure, stopping, and memory shape the experienced record.

heading: ### How sampling and format shape the evidence {#stopping-is-part-of-the-evidence}
text: The practical question is not only “How many cases did we see?” It is also:

heading: ### Personal histories and perceived safety {#personal-history-becomes-a-reference-class}
text: “Nothing bad happened last time” can be useful evidence, but it does not establish that the next exposure is safe. **Normalcy bias** is a broad label for interpreting a warning through an expectation that familiar conditions will continue. One specific pattern was documented after the Loma Prieta earthquake: households without mainshock damage perceived less aftershock risk and responded less to warnings, a pattern Mileti and O'Brien (1992) called *normalization bias*. Their household study was observational.

heading: ### Disasters and the experience trap
text: Mount Vesuvius, the 2021 eruption on La Palma, and floods in Passau provide vivid teaching cases. A city can go decades without a catastrophic event. Everyday experience then supplies thousands of “safe” observations, while historical and scientific description carries the tail risk. The absence of a recent disaster is evidence about frequency—but not evidence that the hazard is zero.
